title: Psalms of Solomon

stories.title: 📜 Psalms of Solomon
summaryBullets: A collection of eighteen Jewish psalms from the late 1st century BCE, composed in response to Jerusalem’s conquest by Pompey in 63 BCE and not included in later biblical canons.

They blend nationalistic lament, calls for righteousness, and Messianic hope—portraying the Messiah as a righteous, David-like deliverer who will rescue Israel, including the earliest use of the title “Son of David.”
The tone shifts between corporate confession, denunciation of Israel’s leaders, and trust in God’s justice, often urging personal and communal repentance.
Though originally written in Hebrew or Aramaic, the collection survives only in Greek and Syriac manuscripts; they were grouped under Solomon’s name—likely for prestige, not authorship.
crossRefs: Psalm 89:3-4: God says he has made a covenant with his chosen one and sworn to David his servant that his offspring will be established for ever and his throne built up to all generations, the promise these psalms hold against the men who had seized that throne.

Isaiah 11:1-5: A shoot comes out of the stump of Jesse, the Spirit of the LORD rests on him, he judges the poor with righteousness and strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth, phrase for phrase what the seventeenth of these psalms asks God to raise up.

Matthew 21:9: The crowds going before and behind cry Hosanna to the Son of David, using as a settled and public title the words this book is the earliest surviving text to apply to a king still to come.

Deuteronomy 17:14-17: The king Israel may set over herself must not multiply horses for himself, or wives, or silver and gold, the law behind this book's picture of a king who puts no trust in horse or rider or bow.
Psalm 20:7: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God, the older statement of the contrast these psalms make about the king they are waiting for.

Leviticus 16:2: The LORD warns that Aaron must not come at just any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, or he will die, the restriction that makes a foreign general strolling through it the wound these psalms open on.

Psalm 79:1-4: O God, the nations have come into your inheritance, they have defiled your holy temple and given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the air, the older psalm these ones are written in the shape of.

Luke 2:25-32: Simeon is waiting for the consolation of Israel and has been told he will not die before he has seen the Lord's Christ, the same expectation these psalms carry, put in the mouth of a man in Jerusalem who lived to see it answered.

translationNotes.note: The man the opening psalms are about, though they never name him. Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus besieged Jerusalem for three months in 63 BC, was let in by one faction against another, breached the temple court with rams and walked into the Holy of Holies. The second of these psalms then watches him die: his arrogance pierced through on the mountains of Egypt, his body carried about on the waves with no one to bury it. Pompey was killed off the Egyptian coast in 48 BC and left on the beach.

The quarrel that let Rome in was between two Hasmonean brothers, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, each claiming the high priesthood and the throne, and both of them appealing to Pompey to settle it. The eighth of these psalms describes the leading men of the land going out to meet him with joy, telling him his way was blessed and inviting him to come in in peace, and then describes what he did once he was inside the gates.

A heavy beam with an iron head, swung under a roofed shed that kept the crew alive while they worked at the wall. Ezekiel 4:2 has the prophet build a model siege in miniature, with a mound, camps and battering rams set against it, and Ezekiel 21:22 has the ram brought against the gates of Jerusalem. The first of these psalms opens on walls beaten down by a siege engine.

The inner room, entered by one man on one day of the year and no oftener. Exodus 26:33 has the veil divide it from the Holy Place, Leviticus 16:2 warns Aaron he will die if he comes in at the wrong time, and Hebrews 9:7 says the high priest went in alone once a year and never without blood. That is what makes a foreign general walking through it the injury these psalms keep pressing on.

Anointed. Oil was poured over a man's head to put him into office. Exodus 29:7 anoints the high priest, Leviticus 8:12 shows it done to Aaron, and 1 Samuel 16:13 has Samuel anoint David out of the horn of oil in front of his brothers. The LORD's anointed is the everyday phrase for the reigning king. The seventeenth of these psalms turns it toward a king who has not come yet.

This book is the earliest surviving text to use the phrase as a title for the coming king rather than as a statement of ancestry. By the time of the Gospels it is settled enough that a crowd can shout it: Matthew 21:9 at the entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 15:22 from the Canaanite woman, Mark 10:47 from blind Bartimaeus at the roadside. Matthew 22:41-45 has Jesus put the title itself to the Pharisees as a question.

The reason most readers open this book. It sets the covenant with David against the men who had taken the throne, then asks God to raise up their king, the son of David, at the time God chooses. It lists what he will do: purge Jerusalem of the nations trampling her, shatter unrighteous rulers, gather a holy people, judge the tribes, put no trust in horse or rider or bow, strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and rule a people made holy, himself taught by God and free from sin.

translationNotes.term: Struck with the word of his mouth
translationNotes.note: Not a figure this book invented. Isaiah 11:4 has the shoot from the stump of Jesse strike the earth with the rod of his mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of his lips. Revelation 19:15 uses the same picture, a sharp sword coming out of the mouth of the rider on the white horse. It is how a text says a king conquers with no weapon in his hand.

translationNotes.term: No trust in horse and rider
translationNotes.note: The law forbade the king to build up a cavalry arm at all. Deuteronomy 17:16 says he must not multiply horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to get more of them. Psalm 20:7 draws the contrast, some in chariots and some in horses but we in the name of the LORD our God, and Psalm 33:16-17 says no king is saved by a great army and a war horse is a false hope for victory.

These psalms sort everyone into two camps and use the words as party labels. The devout or holy ones stand on one side and the sinners on the other, and the sinners are Israel's own rulers and priests rather than foreigners. Psalm 1:1-6 draws the same line between the righteous and the wicked, and the canonical psalter is arranged around it from its first line.

Training that includes correction, the kind a father gives a son he intends to keep. These psalms read the suffering of the righteous as that rather than as abandonment. Proverbs 3:11-12 tells the reader not to despise the LORD's discipline, because the LORD reproves the one he loves as a father the son in whom he delights, and Hebrews 12:5-11 quotes those verses and builds an entire argument on them.

The scattering, and also the scattered people themselves. These psalms speak of Israel driven out to the ends of the earth and ask God to gather her home. Deuteronomy 28:64 gives the threat, that the LORD will scatter you among all peoples from one end of the earth to the other. John 7:35 has the crowd wonder whether Jesus means to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks, and James 1:1 is addressed to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion.

The oldest witness to this book is not a copy of it but a table of contents. The index at the front of Codex Alexandrinus, written in the fifth century, lists the Psalms of Solomon at the very end of the volume, after the New Testament and the letters of Clement, set off from the books above it by a space. The leaves themselves are gone: the end of the codex was torn away, and what it held is lost.

translationNotes.term: Written in Hebrew, kept in Greek
translationNotes.note: These psalms were composed in Hebrew and no Hebrew copy survives. They are preserved in eleven Greek manuscripts of the eleventh to sixteenth centuries and in four Syriac manuscripts, and none of them is complete. The first printed edition came out in 1626 from the Jesuit Juan Luis de la Cerda, and Oscar von Gebhardt's critical edition of 1895 added three manuscripts nobody had known were there.

The heading a psalm carries above its first line, naming an author, an occasion or a tune. The canonical psalter is full of them, as over Psalm 3 and Psalm 51, which name David and the events they belong to. The headings on this collection are the whole reason Solomon's name sits on the book. Nothing inside the psalms themselves mentions him, his reign or his temple.

The second of these psalms watches the conqueror's body carried about on the waves with nobody to bury it, and presents that as the judgment. Burial was not optional. Deuteronomy 21:22-23 requires even an executed criminal to be taken down and buried the same day, and Jeremiah 22:19 pronounces on Jehoiakim the burial of a donkey, dragged out and thrown beyond the gates of Jerusalem.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Psalms of Solomon give voice to first-century BCE Jewish hopes amid oppression, urging moral reform and Messianic deliverance.

intro:
The Psalms of Solomon are eighteen psalms transmitted under Solomon's name. The name comes from the superscriptions the manuscripts carry and from the canon lists; nothing inside the psalms mentions Solomon, his reign, or his temple, and the events they respond to happened nine centuries after him. Those events fix the date. Psalm 2 opens on a sinner who battered down fortified walls with a siege engine and on foreign nations who climbed onto the altar of God (2:1-2). Psalm 8 describes a ruler summoned from the end of the earth whom the leading men of the land went out to meet with joy, telling him his way was blessed and inviting him to enter in peace; he came in as a father enters the house of his sons, and then took the city and killed in its streets (8:15-21). Psalm 17 speaks of a lawless man who laid the land waste and drove out its people. Pompey besieged Jerusalem for three months in 63 BC, was let in by one faction against another, breached the temple court with rams, and walked into the Holy of Holies. Psalm 2 then watches him die: God showed the psalmist his arrogance pierced through on the mountains of Egypt, his body carried about on the waves with none to bury him (2:26-27). Pompey was killed off the Egyptian coast in 48 BC and left unburied on the beach. Psalm 2 was therefore written after 48 BC, and the collection belongs to the middle decades of the first century BC. The psalms are not a chronicle of those events; they read them as judgment on Jerusalem's own leaders, and much of the collection is confession, complaint about the rulers of the sanctuary, and a defense of God's justice.

Psalm 17 is the reason most readers open the book. It sets the covenant with David against the men who had seized the throne, then asks God to "raise up for them their king, the son of David," at the time God chooses, to reign over Israel (17:21). It describes what he will do: purge Jerusalem of the nations that trample her, shatter unrighteous rulers, gather a holy people, judge the tribes, take no trust in horse or rider or bow, strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and rule a people made holy, himself taught by God and free from sin. The psalm calls him christos kyriou, the Lord Messiah (17:32). This is the earliest surviving text to use "son of David" as a title for the coming king.

The psalms were composed in Hebrew, and no Hebrew copy survives. They are preserved in eleven Greek manuscripts of the eleventh to sixteenth centuries and in four Syriac manuscripts, none of them complete. The editio princeps was printed in 1626 by the Jesuit Juan Luis de la Cerda, from a copy of a Greek manuscript that the Augsburg librarian David Hoeschel had brought to notice; Oscar von Gebhardt's critical edition of 1895 added three manuscripts previously unknown. The oldest witness is a table of contents. The index at the front of Codex Alexandrinus, written in the fifth century, lists the Psalms of Solomon at the very end of the volume, after the New Testament and the letters of Clement, separated from the books above it by a space. The leaves themselves are gone; the end of the codex was torn away, and the text it once held is lost. The Stichometry of Nicephorus, from the ninth century, lists the Psalms and Odes of Solomon together at 2,100 lines among the antilegomena, the disputed books. No communion receives the Psalms of Solomon as canonical.

Readers confuse this book with the Odes of Solomon, and the manuscripts encourage it. Ancient lists count the two as one entry, and the Syriac manuscript J. Rendel Harris identified in 1909 carries the Odes first and the Psalms of Solomon after them. They are different books: eighteen Jewish psalms written in Hebrew in the first century BC, and forty-two Christian hymns.
